name: Operational Excellence (OPS)
description: Operate, monitor, upgrade, and continuously improve Couchbase clusters and the applications that use them.

questions.title: How do you notice a problem before users do?
questions.description: Watch resident ratio, latency, and failed cluster tasks, and page someone.

options.label: Watch resident ratio, Key-Value operations per second, and latency

risks.reason: The resident ratio shows how much of a bucket's data is held in memory. When it falls, Couchbase starts serving reads from disk and latency rises. Without a view of resident ratio, throughput, and latency, this change is usually noticed by users before the team.

improvements.title: Monitor the Data Service
improvements.description: We recommend a dashboard and alerts on resident ratio, Key-Value operations per second, and read and write latency per bucket. These are available in the Couchbase Web Console, on the Prometheus metrics endpoint of each node, and in the Capella monitoring views. A steadily falling resident ratio is the earliest sign that the data no longer fits in the memory quota.

options.label: Send cluster metrics to the same place as the rest of the platform

risks.reason: Metrics that live only in the Couchbase Web Console cannot be placed next to application latency during an incident, so it is hard to tell whether a slow request comes from the application or from the database.

improvements.title: Centralize cluster metrics
improvements.description: Consider sending cluster metrics to the same monitoring system as the applications. Couchbase Server exposes a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint on every node, and Capella offers a metrics endpoint that can be scraped as well. One shared timeline makes incident analysis much faster.

options.label: Turn on completed-request logging for slow SQL++ queries

risks.reason: The Query Service keeps a record of slow statements in system:completed_requests, but it only helps when someone reviews it. A slow SQL++ query can consume a large share of Query Service CPU without ever appearing in the application logs.

improvements.title: Record and review slow SQL++ queries
improvements.description: Consider keeping the completed-requests threshold at a value that matches your latency goals and reviewing system:completed_requests regularly, for example after each deployment and whenever query latency changes. Each entry shows the statement, its duration, and the client context id when the application sets one.

options.label: Alert when a node is down, memory headroom is low, or a rebalance fails

risks.reason: Couchbase can fail over a node automatically, but a person still has to find the cause, rebalance, and restore the lost replicas. A rebalance that fails, or memory and disk that run out, also need a person. A dashboard that nobody watches does not page anyone.

improvements.title: Page a person on cluster failures
improvements.description: We recommend alerts that page someone for a node going down, an auto-failover, a failed rebalance, low bucket memory headroom, and low disk space. Couchbase Server includes email alerts for these events and Capella offers alert notifications; both can be forwarded to the on-call tool you already use.

questions.title: How do you add or remove nodes safely?
questions.description: A rebalance moves data. Do it in a quiet window and wait until it finishes.

options.label: Run rebalance in a planned window, not during peak traffic

risks.reason: A rebalance moves vBuckets and index data between nodes over the network and disk. During peak traffic it competes with the application for the same CPU, disk, and network, so both the rebalance and the application slow down.

improvements.title: Plan the rebalance window
improvements.description: Consider scheduling node additions and removals in a quiet window and keeping someone watching until the rebalance reports complete. If a rebalance must be interrupted, it can be stopped from the Web Console and started again later; the data already moved stays in place.

options.label: Use delta recovery when a node was offline briefly and still has its data files

risks.reason: When a node comes back after a short outage, a full recovery copies the entire data set to it again. Delta recovery reuses the data files still on the node and copies only what changed, which makes the rebalance much shorter.

improvements.title: Prefer delta recovery after a short outage
improvements.description: When a node has been down briefly and its disk is intact, consider choosing delta recovery before rebalancing. Full recovery remains the right choice when the disk was replaced or the files cannot be trusted.

options.guidance: Delta recovery is not always possible. It needs the data files that were on the node before it failed.

options.label: Group node additions and removals instead of changing topology one node at a time all week

risks.reason: Every topology change starts its own rebalance. Adding or removing nodes one at a time over several days keeps the cluster moving data for a long time and extends the period of higher load.

improvements.title: Batch topology changes
improvements.description: Where possible, consider adding or removing all the nodes you already know you need in a single change, and letting that one rebalance finish before planning the next.

options.label: Check that rebalance, index builds, and warmup have finished before the next change

risks.reason: A rebalance, an index build, or a warmup can still be running even when the Web Console looks idle. Starting the next change while the previous one is in progress slows both and can make the second change fail.

improvements.title: Check running tasks before the next change
improvements.description: Before the next topology change, consider checking the tasks list in the Web Console (or the /pools/default/tasks REST endpoint) and confirming that rebalance is complete, indexes are online, and warmup has finished.

options.label: After a failover, rebalance or recover the node so the replicas are rebuilt

risks.reason: After a failover, the replicas that were promoted to active are not recreated. Until a rebalance runs, part of the data has fewer copies than configured, and a second failure can lose data.

improvements.title: Rebalance after every failover
improvements.description: Consider adding 'rebalance after failover' to the incident procedure: fix or replace the node, choose delta or full recovery, and rebalance so the configured number of replicas exists again. The Autonomous Operator handles this step automatically, and Capella manages node recovery for you.

questions.title: How do you automate Couchbase deployments and configuration management?
questions.description: Clusters, buckets, indexes, and settings are defined in code and deployed through a pipeline.

options.label: Define clusters, buckets, and roles in code

risks.reason: Settings changed only in the Web Console are not reviewed and are easy to forget. Over time the environments drift apart, and a cluster cannot be rebuilt the same way after a failure.

improvements.title: Keep cluster configuration in code
improvements.description: Consider describing clusters, buckets, memory quotas, users, and roles in code, for example with the Capella Terraform provider, the Autonomous Operator resources, Ansible, or the REST API. Reviewed configuration is easier to audit and to rebuild.

options.label: Run Couchbase on Kubernetes with the Autonomous Operator

risks.reason: On Kubernetes without the Autonomous Operator, upgrades, failover, and rebalance have to be done by hand, and a pod restart can leave the cluster in an unexpected state.

improvements.title: Use the Autonomous Operator
improvements.description: We recommend running Couchbase on Kubernetes through the Couchbase Autonomous Operator, which creates the pods, keeps the cluster at the declared size, and performs upgrades, failover, and rebalance. Direct changes with kubectl are best kept for diagnosis only.

options.label: Keep index definitions in source control and deploy them in a pipeline, never from a framework at runtime

risks.reason: Index definitions applied by hand, or created by a framework when the application starts, skip peer review. A poorly chosen index can slow writes and use Index Service memory for a long time before anyone notices.

improvements.title: Deploy index definitions from the pipeline
improvements.description: Consider keeping CREATE INDEX statements in source control next to the application and applying them from the deployment pipeline. It also helps to turn off any framework option that creates indexes automatically at startup.

antiPatterns: Letting Spring Data or a similar framework create a primary index when the application starts

options.label: Keep memory quotas, bucket settings, and XDCR configuration in source control

risks.reason: When memory quotas, bucket settings, and XDCR configuration exist only in the cluster, it is difficult to know what changed, when, and by whom, and there is no easy way back to a known good configuration.

improvements.title: Version the operational settings
improvements.description: Consider keeping a versioned record of cluster settings: memory quotas per service, bucket settings such as replicas and storage engine, auto-failover settings, and XDCR replications. The REST API and the Capella Management API make it practical to export the current settings and compare them.

options.label: Run integration tests against a real Couchbase instance, not a mock

risks.reason: A mocked database does not reproduce durability, timeouts, scan consistency, or CAS behavior. Problems that only occur against a real cluster then appear in production.

improvements.title: Test against a real Couchbase instance
improvements.description: Consider running the critical paths against a real Couchbase instance in the pipeline, for example with the official Docker image, Testcontainers, or a Capella development cluster.

questions.title: How do you respond to operational events and database incidents?
questions.description: Written procedures for failover, node replacement, restore, and investigation, so incidents are handled the same way every time.

options.label: Write the steps for failover, node replacement, and restore

risks.reason: A failover or restore done under pressure without a written procedure is where mistakes happen: a graceful failover becomes a hard failover, or a restore targets the wrong bucket.

improvements.title: Write the cluster runbooks
improvements.description: We recommend written procedures for graceful failover, hard failover, adding a replacement node, recovery (delta or full), and restoring from backup, with the roles allowed to run each step. Testing them once in a non-production cluster makes them trustworthy.

options.label: Write how to investigate slow queries, high indexer CPU, and XDCR lag

risks.reason: Without an agreed sequence of checks, two people investigating the same incident look in different places, and time is lost before the real cause is found.

improvements.title: Write the investigation steps
improvements.description: Consider a short investigation guide per symptom: slow SQL++ queries (system:completed_requests and EXPLAIN), high Index Service memory or CPU, a growing disk write queue, and XDCR lag. Each guide lists the first metrics and logs to look at.

options.label: Review serious incidents and record what will change

risks.reason: When a serious incident is closed without a written cause and a follow-up change, the same failure tends to come back.

improvements.title: Review serious incidents
improvements.description: After a serious outage, it helps to record the timeline, the root cause, and the change that should prevent a repeat, and to track that change to completion.

questions.title: How do you upgrade while the cluster stays online?
questions.description: Swap in nodes on the new version. Check the SDK before you start.

options.label: Upgrade online with a swap rebalance, one node at a time

risks.reason: Restarting every node at once takes the whole cluster offline. Couchbase Server is designed to be upgraded one node at a time while the cluster keeps serving traffic.

improvements.title: Upgrade online with a swap rebalance
improvements.description: The usual approach is a swap rebalance: add a node on the new version with the same services, remove one old node, rebalance, and repeat. For upgrades from 7.1 or 7.2 to 7.6.0 or 7.6.1, Index Service nodes must be upgraded this way. On Capella and with the Autonomous Operator, the online upgrade is performed for you.

options.label: Check the SDK support matrix before the server upgrade

risks.reason: Each SDK release supports a documented range of server versions. An SDK that is too old for the new server may fail to connect or may fail on specific operations after the upgrade.

improvements.title: Match the SDK to the server version
improvements.description: Before the server upgrade, consider comparing each application's SDK version with the compatibility table in the SDK documentation for the target server version, and planning SDK upgrades first where needed.

options.label: Run the real queries and data shape in a test cluster before the upgrade

risks.reason: A server upgrade can change how a SQL++ query is planned. A test that does not run the production queries and data shape will not reveal a plan that became slower.

improvements.title: Test the upgrade with production-like work
improvements.description: Consider restoring a recent backup, or a masked copy, into a test cluster on the target version and running the important queries and write paths against it before the production upgrade.

options.label: Check indexes, balance, and application errors after the upgrade

risks.reason: An upgrade can look finished in the Web Console while an index is still building or an application has started returning new errors.

improvements.title: Check the cluster after the upgrade
improvements.description: After the upgrade, it helps to confirm that the rebalance is complete, all indexes are online, replication is healthy, and the application error rate and latency are back to their normal level.

options.label: Pin SDK versions and upgrade them on a cadence against the SDK support policy

risks.reason: Couchbase publishes a support window for each SDK version. Checking only at server upgrade time leaves applications on SDK releases that are already out of support and missing fixes.

improvements.title: Track SDK versions like any other runtime
improvements.description: Consider recording the SDK version used by each service, comparing it with the published SDK support window, and scheduling upgrades like any other runtime dependency.

options.label: Scan the Couchbase SDK and its dependencies for known vulnerabilities

risks.reason: A supported server version does not mean the application's SDK and its dependencies are free of published vulnerabilities.

improvements.title: Include the SDK in dependency scanning
improvements.description: Consider including the Couchbase SDK and the libraries it pulls in within the same dependency vulnerability scan used for the rest of the application.

options.label: Run a Couchbase Server version that is still within its support lifecycle

risks.reason: Every Couchbase Server release has a published end-of-maintenance and end-of-life date. A version past those dates no longer receives fixes or security patches, and support options are limited.

improvements.title: Stay on a supported version
improvements.description: Consider checking the current version against the Couchbase Enterprise Software Support Policy and planning the next upgrade before the end-of-maintenance date. Capella clusters are kept on supported versions for you.

questions.title: How do you continually evaluate and improve your Couchbase operations?
questions.description: Regular reviews of indexes, sizing, and operational trends, together with the application team.

options.label: Schedule regular audits of unused indexes and obsolete buckets

risks.reason: Unused indexes and forgotten buckets keep using memory, disk, and backup space, and every index still has to be updated on each write.

improvements.title: Review unused indexes and buckets
improvements.description: Consider a periodic review of index usage, for example through the system:indexes catalog and the index statistics in the Web Console, and removing indexes and buckets that no longer serve an active query or application.

options.label: Review upcoming queries and schema changes with the application team

risks.reason: When the operations team does not hear about upcoming features, new query patterns and data growth arrive without the indexes and capacity they need.

improvements.title: Review the roadmap with the application team
improvements.description: Consider a regular review with the application team to look at upcoming queries, document changes, and expected growth, so index design and capacity can be planned ahead.

options.label: Track and review key operational metrics (e.g., MTTR, failed queries) over time

risks.reason: Without a history of incidents, failed queries, and latency, there is no way to tell whether the changes made are actually reducing downtime or improving performance.

improvements.title: Review operational trends
improvements.description: Consider keeping a few operational measures over time, such as time to recover from incidents, failed or slow queries, and latency at the busiest hour, and reviewing their trend on a regular basis.

options.label: Review CPU, memory, and disk on a schedule and resize the cluster

risks.reason: A cluster sized once and never reviewed is either paying for capacity it does not use or heading toward a limit that nobody is tracking.

improvements.title: Review cluster sizing on a schedule
improvements.description: Consider reviewing CPU, memory, disk, and resident ratio per service on a schedule and comparing them with the Couchbase sizing guidelines, so nodes can be added before a limit is reached or removed when they are not needed.

questions.title: How do you instrument applications that use Couchbase SDKs?
questions.description: See application latency separately from cluster latency, and connect a slow query back to the caller.

options.label: Send SDK traces and metrics to the same system as the application

risks.reason: Cluster dashboards show time spent inside Couchbase, not time spent in the application or on the network. Without SDK tracing a slow request cannot be split into application time and database time.

improvements.title: Trace the SDK calls
improvements.description: Consider enabling the SDK's OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics support and exporting them with the rest of the service. Each Couchbase operation then appears as a span in the same trace as the application code.

options.label: Review SDK threshold logs and orphaned-response reports

risks.reason: The SDK already records operations that exceed a latency threshold and responses that arrive after the operation timed out (orphaned responses). These reports are valuable during an incident but are often never read.

improvements.title: Review SDK threshold and orphan logs
improvements.description: Consider shipping the SDK's threshold and orphan logging output to the same place as application logs, and including them in the first checks after an incident.

options.label: Use ping or diagnostics in application readiness checks

risks.reason: When readiness only checks that the process is running, a service that cannot reach the cluster still receives traffic and fails every request.

improvements.title: Fail readiness when the cluster is unreachable
improvements.description: Consider using the SDK ping or diagnostics call in the readiness check, so the service is only marked ready when it can reach the Couchbase services it depends on.

options.label: Set client_context_id on each SQL++ call so it can be found in completed requests

risks.reason: A slow query seen on the server side cannot be linked to the application request that sent it unless both sides share an identifier.

improvements.title: Pass the request id into SQL++
improvements.description: Consider setting the client_context_id query option from the application's request or trace id. The value then appears in system:completed_requests and in the query logs.

questions.guidance: This question is for the team that owns the service, not the cluster administrators.
antiPatterns: Looking only at cluster dashboards when the latency is inside the client

questions.title: How is the Linux host set up for Couchbase?
questions.description: Couchbase wants RAM. The default Linux settings swap that RAM away and slow the node down.
questions.guidance: Capella manages the host. Answer this for self-managed Server, and for the machines under the Autonomous Operator.

options.label: Set vm.swappiness to 1 on current Linux, and to 0 only on kernels older than 3.5

risks.reason: Most Linux distributions default vm.swappiness to 60, which lets the kernel swap Couchbase memory to disk even when RAM is still available. Swapped memory makes Key-Value operations unpredictably slow.

improvements.title: Set swappiness before the node joins the cluster
improvements.description: Couchbase recommends vm.swappiness set to 1 on current kernels, and to 0 only on kernels older than 3.5. It helps to apply the setting in the image or automation that builds nodes so it survives a reboot.

options.label: Turn transparent huge pages off (enabled and defrag set to never)

risks.reason: Transparent huge pages are enabled by default on many Linux distributions. Couchbase documents that they can cause memory and CPU stalls and recommends turning them off on every node.

improvements.title: Disable transparent huge pages on every Couchbase machine
improvements.description: We recommend setting transparent_hugepage enabled and defrag to never, and making the change persistent across reboots, for example through a systemd unit or a tuned profile. On Kubernetes this is a setting on the worker node, not in the pod.

options.label: Keep the clocks of all nodes synchronized with NTP

risks.reason: Couchbase relies on the node clock for document expiry and for timestamp-based XDCR conflict resolution. Nodes whose clocks drift apart can expire documents at the wrong time or keep the wrong version of a document.

improvements.title: Synchronize clocks with NTP
improvements.description: Consider running an NTP client on every node, pointing all nodes (and both clusters, when XDCR is used) at the same reference time servers, and monitoring clock drift.

questions.title: How prepared are you to work with Couchbase Support?
questions.description: The support plan, the way to open a ticket, and how to collect logs are known before an incident, not during it.

options.label: Know your support plan, severity levels, and how to open a ticket

risks.reason: During an outage, time is lost finding out who holds the support contract, which severity to use, and where to open the ticket.

improvements.title: Record the support path in the runbooks
improvements.description: Consider recording the support plan, the severity definitions, and the ticket URL in the runbooks. Capella includes a Support section in the UI; Couchbase Server customers use the Couchbase Support portal.

options.label: Know how to collect diagnostics from every node (Collect Information or cbcollect_info)

risks.reason: A support investigation starts with the logs from every node. Collecting them for the first time during an incident, on a cluster that is already under pressure, delays the analysis.

improvements.title: Practice log collection before you need it
improvements.description: Consider trying log collection once in advance: in the Web Console under Logs > Collect Information, or with the cbcollect_info tool on each node. The archive can be uploaded directly to Couchbase Support from the collection dialog.

options.label: Keep a current record of versions, topology, buckets, and SDKs in use

risks.reason: Support and your own team need the server version and edition, the services on each node, the bucket settings, and the SDK versions. Without that record, every incident starts by rediscovering it.

improvements.title: Keep a cluster fact sheet
improvements.description: Consider keeping a short, current record per cluster: server version and edition, node count and services per node, buckets with replicas and storage engine, and the SDK version of each application.

name: Security (SEC)
description: Protect identities, network access, data in transit and at rest, certificates, and application credentials.

questions.title: How do you manage identities and permissions for people and machines accessing Couchbase?
questions.description: Administrators sign in through the company directory, and every user has only the permissions it needs.

options.label: Sign administrators in through the Capella organization identity provider

risks.reason: Local Capella accounts that are not tied to the company identity provider are easy to leave behind when people change roles or leave. Access reviews then depend on memory rather than on the directory.

improvements.title: Use organization single sign-on
improvements.description: Consider configuring single sign-on for the Capella organization through your identity provider, so onboarding and offboarding follow the company process. For any remaining non-SSO users, Capella offers multi-factor authentication, and Organization Owners can see each user's MFA status.

options.label: Sign administrators in through LDAP or SAML

risks.reason: Local cluster administrator accounts are easy to leave enabled after a person leaves. Linking administrators to LDAP or SAML ties access to the company directory.

improvements.title: Use LDAP or SAML for administrators
improvements.description: Consider configuring LDAP or SAML authentication for people who administer the cluster, and keeping local accounts for applications only. PAM authenticates against local operating-system accounts and is not a directory.

options.label: Grant each user only the scopes and collections it needs, never a cluster-wide admin role

risks.reason: A user with Full Admin, Cluster Admin, or bucket-wide Application Access can read and change data it has no need for. If that credential leaks, the whole cluster is exposed.

improvements.title: Limit each user to its data
improvements.description: Consider creating roles scoped to the scopes and collections each user actually uses, for example Data Reader and Data Writer on a specific collection. Couchbase RBAC supports this on Server 7.0 and later and on Capella.

options.label: Rotate database passwords on a schedule

risks.reason: A database password that never changes stays valid after a person leaves or a configuration file is copied somewhere it should not be.

improvements.title: Rotate database credentials
improvements.description: Consider storing database credentials in a secrets manager and rotating them on a schedule. Creating the new credential before removing the old one lets applications switch without downtime.

options.label: Give Capella API keys a limited role, an expiry date, and an allowed IP list

risks.reason: A Capella Management API key with Organization Owner privileges, no expiry, and no IP restriction is a long-lived credential that can create or delete clusters from anywhere if it leaks.

improvements.title: Scope the Capella API keys
improvements.description: Consider creating API keys with only the roles the automation needs, keeping the default expiry (180 days) or shorter, restricting the allowed IP addresses, and rotating keys before they expire.

questions.title: How do you detect and investigate security events in your Couchbase environment?
questions.description: Audit logging is on and the logs leave the node, so a change can be traced to a person and a time.

options.label: Turn on auditing for logins and administrative changes

risks.reason: Without an audit record, a changed password, role, or bucket setting cannot be traced to a person or a time.

improvements.title: Enable audit logging
improvements.description: Consider enabling Couchbase auditing for authentication and administrative events. On Capella, audit logging is enabled in the cluster settings and the logs can be exported; on Server, auditing is configured under Security and writes to an audit log on each node.

options.label: Send audit and server logs off the cluster

risks.reason: Logs that exist only on a node are lost when the node is replaced, and are hard to search across nodes during an incident.

improvements.title: Forward logs off the node
improvements.description: Consider forwarding audit and server logs to your central log platform. On self-managed clusters a log shipper on each node is the usual approach; on Capella, audit logs can be exported from the cluster settings or through the Management API.

questions.title: How do you protect your Couchbase network resources?
questions.description: Only known networks reach the data ports and the administration console.

options.label: Allow database and admin traffic only from known networks

risks.reason: A Data Service port or the administration console reachable from the internet can be scanned and attacked.

improvements.title: Close the cluster to unknown networks
improvements.description: On Capella, consider keeping the Allowed IP list limited to the application and administrator networks, and avoiding 'allow access from anywhere'. On self-managed clusters, consider security groups or firewall rules so only application networks reach the data ports and only the administration network reaches the console.

options.label: On Capella, connect from the private network instead of the public endpoint

risks.reason: Traffic to the public Capella endpoint travels over the internet, even when it is encrypted. A private connection keeps it inside the cloud provider's network.

improvements.title: Use a private Capella connection
improvements.description: Consider VPC peering or a private endpoint (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, or Google Private Service Connect) for application traffic, and restricting public access on the cluster once every client has a private path.

questions.title: How do you protect Couchbase data in transit and at rest?
questions.description: Data is encrypted on the network and on disk, with field-level encryption for the most sensitive fields.

options.label: Require TLS for clients and for traffic between nodes

risks.reason: A client or replication connection without TLS can expose credentials and documents to anyone on the network path.

improvements.title: Require TLS
improvements.description: Consider requiring TLS 1.2 or later for clients, and on self-managed clusters enabling node-to-node encryption as well. Capella already encrypts client and inter-node traffic.

options.label: Encrypt data at rest

risks.reason: A disk, volume, or backup that is not encrypted can be read by anyone who obtains a copy of the files.

improvements.title: Encrypt stored data
improvements.description: Capella encrypts data at rest by default and supports customer-managed keys where policy requires that you hold the key. On self-managed clusters, encrypting the disks or volumes is the usual approach; recent versions of Couchbase Server also offer native encryption at rest.

options.label: Encrypt specific fields in the application when the database administrator must not be able to read them

risks.reason: Volume encryption does not hide a field from someone who can run a query. Field-level encryption in the SDK does, for the fields you choose.

improvements.title: Encrypt the fields that must stay hidden
improvements.description: For fields such as national identifiers or secrets, consider the SDK field-level encryption library. Encrypted fields cannot be filtered on in SQL++, so it is best to decide which fields need it during data design.

options.guidance: Use this for fields such as national identifiers or secrets. It is not required for every document.

options.label: If you use XDCR, secure the replication with full TLS encryption

risks.reason: By default, XDCR sends data between clusters without encryption. A half-secure replication protects the password only; a fully secure replication encrypts both authentication and data with TLS.

improvements.title: Use fully secure XDCR replication
improvements.description: Consider selecting the Full (TLS encrypt password and data) option on the XDCR remote cluster reference and providing the destination cluster's root certificate. Replications to a Capella cluster use this setting.

options.guidance: Only relevant when the cluster replicates to another cluster with XDCR.

questions.title: How do you prepare for and respond to security incidents involving Couchbase?
questions.description: Backups are protected, and an emergency administrator path exists for when the identity provider is down.

options.label: Encrypt backups and store them where the cluster cannot overwrite them

risks.reason: A backup that the same account can delete offers little protection after a mistake or a ransomware event, and an unencrypted backup is a second, unprotected copy of the data.

improvements.title: Protect the backup copies
improvements.description: Consider encrypting backups (cbbackupmgr supports encrypted repositories) and storing them in a location with its own credentials and a retention lock where the platform offers one. Capella backups are encrypted and managed for you.

options.label: Keep a tested emergency admin path for when the identity provider is down

risks.reason: When every administrator signs in through an identity provider, an outage of that provider can lock everyone out of the cluster.

improvements.title: Test emergency admin access
improvements.description: Consider keeping one emergency administrator credential in a vault, limiting who can retrieve it, and testing the sign-in on a schedule so it works when needed.

questions.title: How do applications authenticate and connect securely?
questions.description: Each service has its own identity, a secret that is not in source control, and a verified TLS connection.

options.label: Give each service its own least-privilege database user, never Administrator or a shared user

risks.reason: A shared or Administrator credential means every service can read and change every bucket, and a leak in one service exposes all the data.

improvements.title: Create one database user per service
improvements.description: Consider one database user per service, with roles limited to the scopes and collections that service actually uses.

options.label: Load application credentials from a secrets manager at runtime

risks.reason: A password kept in a configuration file or in source control ends up in every environment, every backup, and every log archive.

improvements.title: Fetch the database password at startup
improvements.description: Consider loading the database credential from a secrets manager when the process starts, and keeping it out of source control and build artifacts.

options.label: Connect with couchbases:// and certificate verification left on

risks.reason: A trust-all or insecure TLS setting copied from a development laptop accepts any certificate in production, which lets an attacker on the network path read the traffic.

improvements.title: Require verified TLS
improvements.description: Consider connecting with the couchbases:// scheme and leaving certificate verification enabled. The cluster's CA certificate can be installed in the application's trust store; on Capella it can be downloaded from the cluster's Connect page.

options.label: Use a client certificate instead of a password where the platform supports mutual TLS

risks.reason: A password is a secret that anyone who holds it can use. A client certificate ties the connection to a specific service identity.

improvements.title: Use mutual TLS where it is supported
improvements.description: Where supported, consider client certificate authentication with one certificate per service. When all clients present certificates, the cluster setting for client certificate authentication can be set to mandatory.

options.guidance: A unique user and a verified couchbases:// connection are the required controls. Mutual TLS is an additional option.

questions.guidance: Role-based access on the cluster is necessary, and it does not by itself describe how the application obtains its identity.

questions.title: How do you build secure application code on Couchbase?
questions.description: SQL++ is built with parameters, SDK logs do not contain document bodies, and review looks for Couchbase-specific mistakes.

options.label: Pass SQL++ values as named or positional parameters, never by concatenating user input

risks.reason: Building a SQL++ statement by concatenating user input is an injection vulnerability. It also changes the statement text on every call, so the Query Service cannot reuse a prepared plan.

improvements.title: Parameterize every SQL++ statement
improvements.description: Consider passing user input only as named or positional parameters in the query options, and keeping the statement text itself constant.

options.label: Configure SDK log redaction so documents and personal data are not written to logs or traces

risks.reason: A debug log that prints a document body becomes a second, unmanaged copy of personal data.

improvements.title: Redact SDK and application logs
improvements.description: Consider enabling the SDK log redaction setting and keeping document contents out of application traces and logs.

options.label: In code review, reject a primary index, a collection-wide scan, and a query with no limit

risks.reason: A query that reads an entire collection returns more data than the feature needs and can overload the Query Service, especially as the data grows.

improvements.title: Add Couchbase checks to code review
improvements.description: Consider adding three checks to code review: no primary index in production, no statement whose EXPLAIN plan scans a whole collection, and no SQL++ statement without a LIMIT when it can return many rows.

questions.title: How do you manage TLS certificates?
questions.description: Production uses certificates from your own CA, expiry dates are tracked, and a rotation does not surprise the applications.
questions.guidance: Capella issues and renews the cluster certificate for you. On Capella, only the client trust store item applies.

options.label: Use certificates issued by your organization's CA in production, not the self-signed default

risks.reason: Couchbase Server generates a self-signed certificate at installation. In production, clients cannot verify it against a trusted CA, which pushes teams to disable certificate verification in the SDK.

improvements.title: Issue node certificates from your organization's CA
improvements.description: Consider uploading your organization's root and intermediate CA certificates to the cluster and issuing a certificate for each node from that CA. Applications then verify the connection with a CA they already trust.

options.label: Track certificate expiry and rotate certificates before they expire

risks.reason: An expired node certificate breaks client connections and node-to-node encryption at the same time. Couchbase Server raises an alert 30 days before a certificate expires, but only when alerts are enabled and someone receives them.

improvements.title: Plan certificate rotation ahead of expiry
improvements.description: Consider recording the expiry dates of the root, intermediate, and node certificates, keeping the certificate-expiry alert enabled, and planning the rotation well before the date. Rotation on the server side does not require a restart; the client trust stores need the new CA as well.

options.label: Distribute the cluster CA certificate to applications through a managed trust store

risks.reason: When each application copies the CA certificate by hand, a CA rotation becomes a coordinated change across every service, and a service that is missed fails at its next connection.

improvements.title: Manage the CA certificate centrally
improvements.description: Consider distributing the CA certificate through the platform's trust store or secrets manager, so a rotation is a single change. On Capella, the certificate is available from the cluster's Connect page and through the Management API.

name: Reliability (REL)
description: Survive the loss of a node, a rack, a zone, or a datacenter, and make sure applications recover together with the cluster.

questions.title: How do you survive a lost node, rack, or zone?
questions.description: Replicas, separate failure domains, and enough nodes to fail one over.

options.label: Set a replica count that matches how many nodes you can lose

risks.reason: A bucket with no replicas loses access to the documents on a node as soon as that node is lost, and auto-failover will not fail that node over, because doing so would lose data.

improvements.title: Set replicas on production buckets
improvements.description: We recommend at least one replica on every production bucket. Two replicas add protection when the cluster has enough nodes to place them in separate failure domains. Durable writes are not supported on buckets with three replicas.

options.label: Place the active copy and its replicas in different racks or availability zones

risks.reason: When the active document and its replica sit in the same rack or availability zone, a single failure removes both copies.

improvements.title: Separate copies across failure domains
improvements.description: On self-managed Server, consider defining Server Groups, one per rack or zone, so replicas are placed in a different group from the active copy. Capella spreads nodes across zones when the cluster is deployed in a multi-zone configuration.

options.label: Run production on at least three nodes

risks.reason: Couchbase Server only performs auto-failover in clusters of three or more nodes, because with fewer nodes it cannot tell a failed node from a network split.

improvements.title: Use three or more nodes in production
improvements.description: We recommend three or more nodes for production. One- and two-node clusters are suitable for development. If a third data node is not possible, an arbiter node can provide the extra vote.

options.label: Keep the same number of nodes in each server group

risks.reason: When server groups have different sizes, the smaller group holds a larger share of replica data, runs hotter, and takes more load after a failover.

improvements.title: Balance the server groups
improvements.description: Consider placing the same number of Data Service nodes in each server group. Capella places nodes evenly across zones for you.

options.label: If you have two server groups, add a third group with an arbiter so failover can reach a majority

risks.reason: With two equal server groups, losing one group leaves exactly half the nodes, which is not a majority, so auto-failover does not run.

improvements.title: Add an arbiter in a third group
improvements.description: Consider a third server group containing an arbiter node, which runs only the Cluster Manager and holds no data. It can be a small instance placed in its own rack, host, or zone.

options.guidance: Skip this when you already have three or more equal groups. The arbiter is the vote, not a place to store data.

options.label: Set auto-failover long enough to ignore a short network blip, and short enough to recover

risks.reason: Auto-failover triggers after a node has been unresponsive for the configured timeout; the default is 120 seconds. A value that is too short can fail over a healthy node during a brief network blip, and a value that is too long leaves clients waiting.

improvements.title: Set the auto-failover timeout deliberately
improvements.description: Consider choosing the timeout with the application timeouts in mind and recording why the value was chosen. Values of only a few seconds increase the risk of unnecessary failovers.

options.label: Choose durability levels that the replica and node count can actually satisfy

risks.reason: A durability level the topology cannot satisfy returns a DurabilityImpossible error. For example, majority needs at least two Data Service nodes with one replica, and durable writes are not supported on buckets with three replicas.

improvements.title: Match durability to the topology
improvements.description: Consider checking each write's durability level against the bucket's replica count and the number of Data Service nodes, including the situation where one node is down.

options.label: Keep documents at or under 20 MB and keys at or under 250 bytes

risks.reason: Couchbase Server rejects a document value larger than 20 MB and a key longer than 250 bytes (246 bytes in collections other than the default collection). Discovering this in production means the write path was not validated.

improvements.title: Enforce the document and key limits
improvements.description: Consider validating document size and key length in the application, and designing documents so they stay well below the limit. Arrays that grow without bound are the usual cause of oversized documents.

options.label: Create indexes with replicas so queries keep working when an Index node is lost

risks.reason: An index with no replica becomes unavailable as soon as the Index Service node that holds it fails, and every query that depends on it returns errors until the node is recovered. Index replication is available in Enterprise Edition and on Capella.

improvements.title: Add replicas to production indexes
improvements.description: Consider creating indexes with num_replica set to 1 (or setting a default number of index replicas) so a copy exists on another Index node. The Query Service switches to the replica automatically. The number of replicas must be smaller than the number of Index Service nodes.

questions.title: How do applications handle a short cluster outage?
questions.description: Let the SDK retry. Do not add a second retry loop.

options.label: Rely on the SDK default retry strategy and do not stack an application retry loop on top

risks.reason: The SDK already retries retryable failures until the operation times out (the BestEffortRetryStrategy). An extra application retry loop on top multiplies the load on a cluster that is already struggling, and retrying a write whose outcome is unknown can duplicate data.

improvements.title: Rely on the SDK retry strategy
improvements.description: Consider relying on the SDK retry strategy and the operation timeout rather than wrapping each call in another loop. A write that is not idempotent is best retried only after an error that clearly says it did not happen.

options.guidance: BestEffortRetryStrategy is already the default in SDK 3. Retry a non-idempotent write only when the failure is unambiguous.
antiPatterns: Adding a second retry loop around every SDK call
Retrying a write after an ambiguous timeout

options.label: Read from a replica when the active copy is unavailable and a slightly older document is acceptable

risks.reason: During a failover, a read of the active copy waits until the failover completes. A replica read can return the last replicated version sooner, which may be slightly older.

improvements.title: Add a replica read for that path
improvements.description: For reads that can accept slightly stale data, consider getAnyReplica or getAllReplicas as a fallback. Reads that must see the latest write should keep using the active copy.

options.guidance: Replica reads can return data that is one replication behind the active document.

options.label: Make writes safe to retry, or do not retry them when the result is unknown

risks.reason: Retrying a write whose result was lost, for example after a timeout, can create a second document or apply the same business action twice.

improvements.title: Decide which writes are safe to retry
improvements.description: Consider using a stable document key so a repeated insert is detected, and retrying a write only when the error states the write did not happen or when repeating it does not change the outcome.

questions.title: How do you manage disaster recovery across different datacenters?
questions.description: A second site is a business decision. If the service must survive the loss of one datacenter, the copy in the other site has to be real, measured, and tested.

options.label: If a second site is required, replicate to it with XDCR and record the conflict mode

risks.reason: Backups restore data to a point in time; they do not keep a second site current. If the business needs a live second site, XDCR is the Couchbase mechanism for it. The conflict-resolution mode is chosen when the bucket is created and cannot be changed afterwards.

improvements.title: Add a second site only when the target requires it
improvements.description: If a second site is required, consider configuring XDCR to the recovery cluster and recording the conflict-resolution mode in the design. If one site is sufficient, recording that decision in the notes is a valid answer.

options.label: Write the recovery point and recovery time, and check the design against them

risks.reason: Without a recovery point objective and a recovery time objective, nobody can judge whether the backup schedule or the replication lag is sufficient.

improvements.title: Write the recovery targets
improvements.description: Consider writing down how much data can be lost and how long the service can be down, then comparing the backup interval, backup retention, and XDCR lag with those numbers.

options.label: If a second site exists, practice the switch

risks.reason: A recovery design that has never been exercised often fails on details such as DNS, connection strings, or application configuration.

improvements.title: Practice the site switch
improvements.description: Consider practicing the switch on a schedule: point a test application at the recovery cluster and confirm the data, the credentials, and the network path.

options.guidance: Check this when a second site exists. A single-site design is recorded in the notes on the previous items.

questions.guidance: Leave these unchecked when a single site is an accepted decision, and write that decision in the notes. They are findings only when a second site is required and missing.

questions.title: How do you back up data and ensure its recoverability?
questions.description: Backups run on a schedule, and a restore has been tested.

options.label: Take scheduled backups and test a restore

risks.reason: A backup that has never been restored is an unverified copy. Accidental deletion, a bad deployment, and disk loss all need a copy that is known to work.

improvements.title: Schedule backups and test a restore
improvements.description: On Capella, consider a backup schedule that matches the recovery objectives (by default, cluster backups run every 4 hours and are kept for 7 days). On self-managed clusters, the Backup Service or cbbackupmgr are the supported tools. Restoring into a non-production bucket on a schedule confirms the backup works.

options.label: Store Data, Index, and Analytics on persistent volumes

risks.reason: An emptyDir or other ephemeral volume is removed when the pod is replaced. The node then has to be rebuilt from replicas or from backup, which takes time and adds load.

improvements.title: Use persistent volumes
improvements.description: In the Autonomous Operator cluster definition, consider persistent volume claims for the Data, Index, Analytics, and Search services. Capella manages storage for you.

options.guidance: Capella manages storage for you. This control applies to clusters run by the Autonomous Operator.

questions.title: How do you manage disk space and compaction?
questions.description: The data disk never fills, compaction runs when it should, and there is room for a rebalance.
questions.guidance: Capella monitors and manages cluster storage for you. Answer this for self-managed Server and for the Autonomous Operator.

options.label: Alert on data disk usage before the disk fills

risks.reason: When the data disk fills, the Data Service can no longer persist writes and the node becomes unhealthy. Couchbase Server includes disk-usage alerts for the data path, but they only help when alerts are enabled and routed to a person.

improvements.title: Alert on disk usage
improvements.description: Consider keeping the Couchbase disk-usage alert enabled and forwarded to on-call, and adding a platform-level alert on free space for the data and index paths.

options.label: Keep auto-compaction enabled, scheduled outside peak hours when needed

risks.reason: Couchstore data files grow with every update until compaction reclaims the space. Auto-compaction is on by default, with a 30% fragmentation threshold. Turning it off, or letting it run at peak on a busy disk, leads to a full disk or slow I/O during business hours.

improvements.title: Review the auto-compaction settings
improvements.description: Consider leaving auto-compaction enabled and, when the disk is shared with heavy traffic, giving it a time window outside peak hours. Magma buckets manage fragmentation differently and need far less tuning.

options.guidance: Mainly for Couchstore buckets. Leave unchecked when every bucket uses Magma.

options.label: Keep disk headroom for compaction, rebalance, and failover

risks.reason: Compaction writes a new file next to the old one, and a failover or rebalance brings more data onto the surviving nodes. A disk that is already near full cannot absorb either.

improvements.title: Size the disk with free space in mind
improvements.description: Consider sizing the data disk with the free space the Couchbase sizing guidelines recommend for compaction, and with room for one node's data to arrive after a failover. It helps to review this as the data grows.

questions.title: How do you manage cluster capacity to prevent resource-induced outages?
questions.description: The cluster has enough memory, CPU, and disk to keep serving after one node is lost.

options.label: Keep enough free memory, CPU, and disk to lose one node

risks.reason: When the remaining nodes cannot hold the replica data and the traffic of a lost node, the failover of one node overloads the rest and can lead to a second failure.

improvements.title: Size for one node down
improvements.description: Consider sizing so the cluster can lose one node and still stay within memory, CPU, and disk limits. The Couchbase sizing guidelines describe how to account for replicas and the working set.

questions.title: How do you test the resiliency of your Couchbase architecture?
questions.description: Stop a node while the application is running, and confirm clients recover.

options.label: On a schedule, stop a node and confirm the cluster recovers

risks.reason: A failover setting that has never been exercised can fail the first time a node is really lost, because of server group, disk, or network details nobody had seen.

improvements.title: Practice a node failure
improvements.description: Consider stopping one node in a non-production cluster on a schedule and confirming that auto-failover, rebalance, and application behavior match expectations.

options.label: Test failover and rebalance under application load, including SDK timeouts and error handling

risks.reason: A cluster drill run without an application does not show whether clients time out, retry correctly, or duplicate writes.

improvements.title: Fail the cluster while the application is serving traffic
improvements.description: During a failover or rebalance test, consider watching client errors, ambiguous timeouts, and retry counts from the application side, not only from the cluster side.

questions.title: How do you manage the SDK connection lifecycle?
questions.description: One cluster connection lives for the life of the process and is shared by every request.

options.label: Create one long-lived Cluster object per process and share it across requests

risks.reason: Opening a new Cluster connection per request is expensive: each one bootstraps, opens sockets, and loads the cluster map. Under load it exhausts connections and adds latency to every call.

improvements.title: Share one Cluster connection
improvements.description: Consider creating the Cluster object once at application startup and sharing it across requests. The SDK is designed to be used this way and is safe to share between threads.

options.label: Call waitUntilReady at startup and fail if the cluster cannot be reached

risks.reason: A process that starts before it can reach Couchbase fails on the first real user request instead of failing the deployment, which is harder to detect.

improvements.title: Wait until the SDK is ready
improvements.description: Consider calling waitUntilReady during startup and failing the deployment if the cluster is not reachable within a reasonable time.

options.label: Bootstrap from DNS SRV or from more than one seed node

risks.reason: A single seed hostname in the connection string is a single point of failure for every new process that needs to join the cluster.

improvements.title: Configure multiple bootstrap targets
improvements.description: Consider a DNS SRV record, or a connection string with several node addresses. Capella connection strings already use DNS SRV.

options.label: In a short-lived function, create the connection outside the handler and reuse it

risks.reason: A function that connects to Couchbase on every invocation spends much of the request on bootstrap and can exhaust cluster connections at scale.

improvements.title: Reuse the connection across invocations
improvements.description: Consider initializing the Cluster object outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it. On Capella, very short functions can also use the Data API, a REST interface that needs no SDK connection.

options.guidance: This applies to any Couchbase cluster behind a short-lived function. The Capella Data API is an extra option on Capella only.

options.label: Close the SDK connection when the application stops

risks.reason: A process that exits without closing the SDK connection leaves sockets open until the server times them out.

improvements.title: Disconnect on shutdown
improvements.description: Consider calling disconnect or close from the application's shutdown hook.

questions.guidance: This is the most common application-side production failure: a new connection for every request.
antiPatterns: new Cluster() inside a web request
A hardcoded single hostname as the only seed

questions.title: How do you set timeouts and handle SDK errors?
questions.description: Each operation has a timeout that fits the caller, and an unknown write result is not treated as a clean failure.

options.label: Set a timeout per operation type that fits the upstream API deadline

risks.reason: The SDK defaults are 2.5 seconds for Key-Value operations and 75 seconds for SQL++ queries. These rarely match the deadline of the API that calls Couchbase, so a request can keep waiting long after the user has given up.

improvements.title: Set explicit timeout budgets
improvements.description: Consider setting Key-Value, durable-write, query, search, and transaction timeouts from the caller's latency budget, either in the cluster environment or per operation.

options.label: Treat an ambiguous failure differently from a failure that is known not to have happened

risks.reason: An AmbiguousTimeout or DurabilityAmbiguous error means the operation may have succeeded. Retrying it blindly can apply a payment, an order, or a stock change twice.

improvements.title: Handle ambiguous errors separately
improvements.description: Consider handling ambiguous errors on their own path: read the document back or reconcile before retrying. Errors that clearly state the operation did not happen can be retried right away.

options.label: If the application retries, use capped exponential backoff with jitter and do not stack it on SDK retries

risks.reason: Immediate retries from both the SDK and the application multiply the load on a cluster that is already unhealthy.

improvements.title: Cap and jitter any extra retry
improvements.description: The SDK retry strategy already uses exponential backoff. If the application adds its own retry, consider a maximum delay, jitter, and a stop condition.

options.label: Bound how many asynchronous or reactive calls are in flight

risks.reason: Unbounded concurrency during a recovery sends more work to a cluster that is still catching up, which delays the recovery.

improvements.title: Limit in-flight SDK calls
improvements.description: Consider a concurrency limit on asynchronous and reactive pipelines, and queueing or shedding work beyond that limit.

options.label: Degrade a read to a replica or to cached data when the primary read times out

risks.reason: A timeout on the active copy becomes a user-facing error even when a replica or a cache could have answered.

improvements.title: Define the fallback read
improvements.description: For read paths that allow it, consider falling back to a replica read or a cached value, and signalling to the caller that the data may be slightly stale.

questions.guidance: An ambiguous timeout means the write may have succeeded. It is not the same error as a document that was not found.
antiPatterns: One timeout value for Key-Value and SQL++

name: Performance Efficiency (PERF)
description: Keep Key-Value and SQL++ access fast through the right access path, indexes, and sizing. Sub-millisecond latency applies to Key-Value access, not to SQL++.

questions.title: How do you keep SQL++ fast?
questions.description: Use an index, avoid functions on indexed fields, and prepare statements that run often.

options.label: Cover frequent SQL++ queries with an index that contains the fields they return

risks.reason: When an index contains only the filter fields, the Query Service must fetch each matching document from the Data Service after the index scan. A covering index returns the result from the index alone and avoids that extra step.

improvements.title: Cover the frequent queries
improvements.description: For frequent queries, consider including the returned fields in the index as well as the filter fields, and confirming with EXPLAIN that the plan no longer contains a Fetch step.

options.label: Do not wrap an indexed field in a function inside WHERE

risks.reason: Applying a function to an indexed field in the WHERE clause, such as LOWER(name) = 'a', prevents the planner from using a bounded index scan on that field. The query then reads a much wider range or falls back to another index.

improvements.title: Keep predicates usable by the index
improvements.description: Consider storing the value in the form you search for, for example a lowercase copy of the field, or creating an index on the same expression that is used in the WHERE clause.

options.label: Use Search for text search instead of many extra secondary indexes

risks.reason: Secondary indexes are a poor fit for ad-hoc text search across many fields. The Search Service is built for that access pattern.

improvements.title: Use Search for text queries
improvements.description: Consider a Search index for the text fields. With a Flex Index, SQL++ can use the Search index transparently when the query qualifies.

options.guidance: Skip this when the workload has no text search.

options.label: Use prepared statements (adhoc false) for SQL++ that runs often with different values

risks.reason: When the same query shape is sent as new statement text each time, the Query Service parses and plans it again on every call.

improvements.title: Prepare statements that run often
improvements.description: Consider keeping the statement text constant with parameters and setting the SDK adhoc option to false, so the Query Service prepares the statement once and reuses the plan.

options.label: Partition very large indexes across Index nodes

risks.reason: A single very large index lives on one Index Service node (plus its replicas), which limits scan throughput and memory to that node.

improvements.title: Partition the large index
improvements.description: Consider PARTITION BY HASH on a large index so it is split across Index Service nodes and scanned in parallel. Index partitioning is an Enterprise Edition feature.

options.guidance: Only for indexes that are too large or too busy for one Index node.

questions.title: How are client data access paths and document models structured?
questions.description: Known documents are read by key, documents are shaped around their access path, and framework-generated SQL++ is reviewed.

options.label: Read and write one known document with a Key-Value call, not with SQL++

risks.reason: Reading a document by its key through SQL++ adds query planning and an index lookup. A Key-Value get or upsert goes directly to the Data Service and is much faster.

improvements.title: Use Key-Value for a known id
improvements.description: When the document id is known, consider the Key-Value API (get, insert, replace, upsert). SQL++ is best kept for finding documents by their fields.

options.label: Shape documents around one access, and update a single field with a Sub-Document call

risks.reason: A document that grows without limit, or an update that rewrites the whole document to change one field, moves more data than necessary on every call.

improvements.title: Match the document to the access
improvements.description: Consider shaping each document around one access path and keeping its size bounded. A Sub-Document mutation (mutateIn) changes a single field without sending the rest of the document.

options.label: Use Eventing instead of polling when the cluster should react to a change

risks.reason: An application that polls for changes adds a steady query load. The Eventing Service runs a function when a document changes, with no polling.

improvements.title: React on the server instead of polling
improvements.description: Where the reaction belongs next to the data, consider moving it into an Eventing function. A message bus remains a valid design when the consumer is outside the cluster.

options.guidance: Polling is the problem. Eventing is one Couchbase option, not the only one.

options.label: Design document keys for direct lookup and avoid a single hot key

risks.reason: A model that can only be read through a query misses the fastest path in Couchbase, the key lookup. A single key that every request updates becomes a hot spot on one node.

improvements.title: Make the common read a key lookup
improvements.description: Consider putting the natural lookup value in the document id, and splitting a hot counter or lock document across several keys when one key receives most of the writes.

options.label: Review framework-generated SQL++ with EXPLAIN and keep primary indexes out of production

risks.reason: Some frameworks and ORMs generate SQL++ that scans a whole collection, or create a primary index at startup. Those queries work on a small data set and slow down as the data grows.

improvements.title: Treat generated SQL++ as production code
improvements.description: Consider capturing the SQL++ a framework sends, running EXPLAIN on it, and treating a plan that uses a primary index or a full scan as a build failure.

options.label: Fetch only the fields the caller needs, with a SQL++ projection or a Sub-Document lookup

risks.reason: Reading a whole document to use one field increases network transfer and client memory.

improvements.title: Project or use lookupIn
improvements.description: Consider selecting only the required fields in SQL++, or using a Sub-Document lookup (lookupIn) when the document key is known.

options.label: Update counters with an atomic increment or decrement

risks.reason: A counter updated by read-modify-write loses updates under concurrency and creates contention on one document.

improvements.title: Use the atomic counter API
improvements.description: Consider the SDK increment and decrement operations, which update a counter atomically on the server.

questions.title: How do you size each Couchbase service?
questions.description: Data, Query, Index, and Search do not want the same hardware.

options.label: Run heavy Query, Index, or Search work on its own nodes when they contend with Data

risks.reason: Query, Index, and Search share CPU and memory with the Data Service when they run on the same nodes, and a heavy query or index build can slow Key-Value latency.

improvements.title: Separate services that contend
improvements.description: Consider placing the Data Service on its own nodes when Query or Index load affects Key-Value latency. Multi-dimensional scaling lets each service scale independently. A small cluster can still share services when measurements show it is fine.

options.label: Give the Index service enough RAM that indexes stay in memory

risks.reason: An index that does not fit in the Index Service memory quota is read from disk, and every query that uses it becomes slower.

improvements.title: Size the Index Service
improvements.description: Consider watching the index resident ratio and the Index Service memory quota, and adding memory or Index nodes before indexes start spilling to disk. The standard index storage engine (Plasma) can keep part of an index on disk, but queries are fastest when the working set is in memory.

options.label: Pick Magma or Couchstore for the size of the bucket

risks.reason: Couchstore is a good fit when the dataset stays in memory. Magma is designed for data sets much larger than memory; it is the default storage engine on Capella and the recommended engine on Couchbase Server 8.0 and later.

improvements.title: Match the storage engine to the bucket
improvements.description: The storage engine is chosen per bucket. Consider Magma for large buckets and for data sets that do not fit in memory, and Couchstore when the working set fits in RAM. Changing the engine later requires a migration, so it is best decided at bucket creation.

options.guidance: Capella uses Magma by default. On Server 8.0 and later, Magma is the recommended engine for most buckets. Couchstore fits a small dataset that stays in memory. Reading a document from disk is still a disk read.

options.label: Keep the total service memory quotas within the Couchbase guideline for the node

risks.reason: Couchbase recommends allocating no more than 90% of a node's memory (80% on nodes with little memory) to Couchbase services. Quotas set higher than that leave nothing for the operating system and for the Couchbase processes that run outside the quotas, which leads to swapping or to the process being killed.

improvements.title: Check service memory quotas against node RAM
improvements.description: Consider reviewing the Memory Quotas panel in the Web Console against the node RAM, and sizing the Data Service quota from the sizing guidelines (metadata, values, replicas, working set, and overhead).

questions.title: How do you maintain optimal query execution plans and database statistics?
questions.description: The query planner needs fresh statistics. The Index Advisor is a helper, not a required control.

options.label: Run UPDATE STATISTICS on collections whose data shape changes

risks.reason: Without up-to-date statistics, the cost-based optimizer has little information about how many documents match a predicate and can choose a poor index or join order.

improvements.title: Refresh collection statistics
improvements.description: Consider running UPDATE STATISTICS on the collections used by complex queries after large loads or significant data changes.

options.label: Use the Index Advisor (ADVISE) when a slow query has no obvious index

risks.reason: The Index Advisor (ADVISE) suggests an index for a given statement. It is a starting point and does not replace EXPLAIN.

improvements.title: Ask ADVISE for a starting index
improvements.description: When a slow query has no obvious index, consider running ADVISE on the statement, then checking the suggestion with EXPLAIN against the indexes that already exist.

options.guidance: A missing visit to the Index Advisor is not itself a defect.

questions.title: How do your client applications efficiently interact with the database cluster?
questions.description: Move many documents in batches, page through large results, and test with realistic data.

options.label: When loading many documents, use the SDK bulk or reactive API with a bounded batch

risks.reason: Sending one document at a time and waiting for each response turns a bulk load into a long sequence of round trips.

improvements.title: Batch large loads
improvements.description: Consider the SDK bulk or reactive APIs with a bounded number of concurrent operations, and choosing the batch size from a test rather than an unlimited loop.

options.guidance: Check this if the application imports or updates many documents. A request that touches one document does not need it.

options.label: Defer index builds while a large import is running

risks.reason: Building every index while millions of documents are loading slows both the import and the index build.

improvements.title: Build indexes after the import
improvements.description: Consider creating indexes with defer_build set to true, loading the data, then running BUILD INDEX so all indexes are built in a single pass.

options.guidance: This applies to a bulk load, not to everyday writes.

options.label: Stream large results and paginate with a keyset instead of a large OFFSET

risks.reason: A large OFFSET still reads and discards every skipped row on each page, so later pages get slower.

improvements.title: Page with a keyset
improvements.description: Consider streaming results from the SDK and paginating from the last key or document id (keyset pagination) rather than increasing OFFSET.

options.label: Set and test batch size and parallelism instead of leaving them unbounded

risks.reason: An unbounded fan-out saturates the cluster during a bulk job and during a recovery.

improvements.title: Cap in-flight work
improvements.description: Consider choosing a batch size and a concurrency limit, and measuring them against a realistic data set.

options.label: Performance-test with realistic document sizes and key distribution

risks.reason: A test with tiny, uniform documents hides the working set size and the hot keys that production will have.

improvements.title: Load-test the real shape of the data
improvements.description: Consider load-testing with production-like document sizes, TTLs, and key distribution, for example with cbc-pillowfight or YCSB.

options.label: Use a Key-Value range scan for key-ordered batch work instead of adding an index only for that job

risks.reason: An index created only so that a batch job can walk through keys adds memory and write cost to the cluster.

improvements.title: Prefer a Key-Value range scan for key ranges
improvements.description: On Couchbase Server 7.6 and later, consider the SDK Key-Value range scan for jobs that only need documents in key order, instead of a secondary index.

questions.title: How do you optimize Full Text Search (FTS) and Analytics workloads?
questions.description: Answer this only if the workload uses Search or Analytics. A cluster with neither service should leave these unchecked.

options.label: Run large analytical scans on Analytics, not on the operational Query Service

risks.reason: A full-collection aggregation on the Query Service uses the same CPU as the application's operational queries.

improvements.title: Move heavy scans to Analytics
improvements.description: Consider running long scans and ad-hoc aggregates on the Analytics Service, which keeps its own copy of the data and does not compete with operational queries.

options.guidance: Skip this when the workload has no analytical scans.

options.label: Partition a Search index that is too large for one node

risks.reason: A single large Search index can use more memory and disk than one Search node can provide.

improvements.title: Partition the large Search index
improvements.description: Consider setting index partitions on the Search index so it is spread across Search nodes.

options.guidance: Only for a Search index that has outgrown one node.

options.label: Index only the Search fields you query, with an explicit type mapping

risks.reason: The default dynamic mapping indexes every field in every document. The Search index then grows with data the application never searches.

improvements.title: Index only the fields you search
improvements.description: Consider defining the document type and only the child fields that Search should index, and disabling the default dynamic mapping.

options.guidance: Only if you use Search.

questions.guidance: Search and Analytics are separate services. They are not required for a Key-Value or SQL++ application.

name: Cost Optimization (COST)
description: Pay for the capacity the workload needs: right-size the infrastructure, manage data lifecycles, and attribute costs.

questions.title: How do you govern and monitor your Couchbase resource usage and costs?
questions.description: Costs are attributed, monitored, and alerted on, and the access pattern is reviewed before capacity is added.

options.label: Identify cost attribution using comprehensive resource tagging

risks.reason: Without tags on the underlying instances, volumes, or Kubernetes resources, the database cost cannot be attributed to the application or business unit that drives it.

improvements.title: Tag the Couchbase infrastructure
improvements.description: Consider agreeing a tagging scheme for the Couchbase infrastructure, so cost reports can be split by application, environment, and owner.

options.label: Alert when cluster cost or size moves outside the expected range

risks.reason: A cluster that scales up, or a network bill that jumps, can run for days before anyone notices.

improvements.title: Alert on cost and size
improvements.description: On Capella, consider reviewing the billing and cluster sizing views regularly. On self-managed clusters in a cloud account, consider alerts on account spend and on unexpected growth in node count.

options.label: Review N+1 queries, polling, and unbounded scans before adding Query or Index nodes

risks.reason: The usual reason a cluster is oversized is the application access pattern, for example N+1 queries, polling loops, or scans of a whole collection, rather than a shortage of nodes.

improvements.title: Fix the access pattern before buying capacity
improvements.description: Before adding Query or Index nodes, consider reviewing system:completed_requests for repeated queries, polling, and full scans, and fixing those patterns first.

options.label: Make per-service usage visible with its own user and collections

risks.reason: A shared cluster where every service uses the same user and collection cannot show which service is driving the cost.

improvements.title: Separate tenants inside the cluster
