improvements.description: Consider giving each service its own database user and its own collections. Per-collection and per-user statistics then show who is using the cluster.

questions.title: How do you optimize Couchbase compute and infrastructure costs?
questions.description: Compute is sized from measured demand and bought with the right pricing model.

options.label: For a steady cloud footprint, use the provider's committed pricing

risks.reason: A database that runs all month on on-demand cloud pricing pays the highest rate for a predictable load.

improvements.title: Price the steady footprint
improvements.description: For the nodes that always run, consider the cloud provider's committed or reserved pricing. This does not apply to hardware you already own.

options.guidance: On-premises hardware does not have a reserved-instance price. Leave this unchecked and note that.

options.label: Scale Capella compute from observed demand rather than a fixed oversized cluster

risks.reason: A Capella cluster sized for a peak that never arrives is paid for all month.

improvements.title: Scale Capella from measured demand
improvements.description: Consider reviewing Capella sizing against CPU, memory, and query load, and resizing when the trend is sustained. Capella can scale nodes and services online.

options.label: Scale Autonomous Operator clusters with Kubernetes autoscaling tied to real service metrics

risks.reason: The Operator can add nodes, but an autoscaling rule based only on CPU ignores Index and Query memory and can either stall the cluster or add nodes that are not needed.

improvements.title: Autoscale the Operator from service metrics
improvements.description: Consider the Autonomous Operator's autoscaling with metrics from the service that is actually saturated, rather than a single cluster-wide CPU target.

options.label: Keep a capacity plan; Couchbase Server has no built-in cluster autoscaler

risks.reason: Couchbase Server has no built-in cluster autoscaler. Waiting for a node to run out of memory and then adding hardware by hand is the common failure mode of self-managed clusters.

improvements.title: Keep a capacity plan for self-managed Server
improvements.description: Consider keeping a capacity plan that tracks headroom and schedules node additions ahead of growth, and automating node provisioning so a planned addition is quick.

questions.title: How do you optimize Couchbase data storage costs?
questions.description: Storage is spent only on data and indexes that are actually used.

options.label: Use an ephemeral bucket only for data that can be dropped on restart

risks.reason: A cache stored in a Couchbase bucket still writes to disk unless the bucket is ephemeral.

improvements.title: Use an ephemeral bucket for a real cache
improvements.description: Consider an ephemeral bucket for data that can be lost on restart. Data that must be kept belongs in a Couchbase bucket.

options.guidance: Most application data should stay in a Couchbase bucket that persists.

options.label: Identify and remove redundant or duplicate indexes

risks.reason: Unused or duplicate indexes consume Index Service memory and disk, and each one still has to be updated on every write.

improvements.title: Remove unused indexes
improvements.description: Consider reviewing index usage statistics on a schedule and dropping indexes that no longer support an active query.

questions.title: How do you manage data transfer and network costs?
questions.description: Data transfer between zones, regions, and the public internet is planned and measured.

options.label: Keep Capella traffic on a private connection so it is not billed as public egress

risks.reason: Traffic from an application to the public Capella endpoint can be billed as internet egress by the cloud provider.

improvements.title: Avoid public egress to Capella
improvements.description: Consider a private endpoint or VPC peering for the application path. This is the cost side of the private-network control in Security.

options.guidance: The security control is the one that must be checked. This item is the cost reason for the same design.

options.label: If you use XDCR across regions, replicate only the data the other region needs

risks.reason: Cross-region replication is billed as data transfer. Copying a whole bucket also copies data the other site may never read.

improvements.title: Filter cross-region replication
improvements.description: Consider filtering the XDCR replication by collection or with a filter expression, so only the required documents cross the region boundary.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when there is no cross-region XDCR.

options.label: On Server 7.6.2 or later, prefer a replica in the same zone when a local copy is acceptable

risks.reason: In cloud pricing, a read that crosses an availability zone can be billed even when a copy exists in the local zone.

improvements.title: Prefer the local zone for replica reads
improvements.description: On Couchbase Server 7.6.2 and later, consider configuring the SDK preferred server group so replica reads favor the local zone. This is for reads that can accept replica data; reads that must see the latest write should keep using the active copy.

options.guidance: On-premises networks may not bill cross-zone traffic. Leave this unchecked when it does not apply.

options.label: Leave SDK compression on and trim payloads with projections or Sub-Document operations

risks.reason: Sending a full document when the caller needs one field increases data-transfer cost.

improvements.title: Send fewer bytes per call
improvements.description: Consider leaving SDK compression enabled (it is on by default) and fetching only the fields the request uses through projections or Sub-Document operations.

questions.title: How do you manage the lifecycle of your Couchbase environments to prevent waste?
questions.description: Non-production clusters are stopped when nobody uses them, and unused assets are removed.

options.label: Turn off or schedule a pause for non-production Capella clusters outside business hours

risks.reason: A development or test Capella cluster that runs all night and all weekend is billed while nobody is using it.

improvements.title: Stop non-production Capella clusters
improvements.description: Consider turning non-production clusters off outside working hours, or scheduling on and off times in Capella. Production clusters should stay on.

options.guidance: Capella exposes cluster on/off and scheduling. Self-managed Server does not have a hibernation feature.

options.label: Audit and remove sample buckets, unused data, and orphaned volumes

risks.reason: Sample buckets, unused data, and detached volumes keep consuming storage without serving any application.

improvements.title: Clean up unused assets
improvements.description: Consider keeping sample buckets out of shared and production clusters, and reviewing orphaned volumes and unused buckets on a schedule.

name: Data Management & Consistency (DATA)
description: Durability, concurrency, consistency, data lifecycle, and how data is organized and replicated.

questions.title: How do you manage write durability and concurrency controls?
questions.description: Writes that matter use a durability level, and concurrent updates use CAS.

options.label: Set a durability level on writes that must survive a node loss

risks.reason: A write that returns before it is replicated can be lost if the active node fails right after. Durability levels make Couchbase wait until the write is held by a majority of the Data Service nodes, or persisted, before acknowledging it.

improvements.title: Set durability on the writes that need it
improvements.description: For writes that must survive a node loss, consider the majority durability level, or a stronger level the topology can meet (majorityAndPersistActive or persistToMajority). Cache-style writes can stay at the default.

options.label: Use the document CAS when two callers can update the same document

risks.reason: A read-modify-write that ignores CAS silently overwrites a change made by another caller in between.

improvements.title: Use CAS for concurrent updates
improvements.description: Consider reading the document, modifying it, and replacing it with the CAS value from the read, then retrying when the server reports a CAS mismatch.

options.label: Use getAndLock only for a proven hot document, and keep the lock short

risks.reason: Using getAndLock as the normal update path holds a lock on the document and lowers throughput. Optimistic locking with CAS is the usual control.

improvements.title: Keep pessimistic locks rare
improvements.description: Consider keeping pessimistic locks for a measured hot document only, with a short lock time, and avoiding a lock held across a call to another system.

options.guidance: Pessimistic locking is the exception. A missing getAndLock is not itself a risk.
antiPatterns: Holding a pessimistic lock across a network call

questions.title: How do you structure data lifecycles and logical isolation?
questions.description: Data is organized into scopes and collections, temporary documents expire with a TTL, and document shapes are versioned.

options.label: Organize datasets logically using Scopes and Collections

risks.reason: Mixing unrelated datasets in one collection complicates index design, access control, and data lifecycle. Creating a separate bucket for each dataset adds memory and management overhead.

improvements.title: Organize data into scopes and collections
improvements.description: Consider grouping data into scopes and collections within a bucket. Roles, indexes, TTL, and XDCR filters can all be set per collection.

options.label: Set a TTL on documents that should disappear, such as sessions and one-time tokens

risks.reason: A cleanup job that deletes old documents can fall behind. A TTL lets the Data Service expire them automatically.

improvements.title: Expire temporary documents with a TTL
improvements.description: Consider a TTL on documents or collections that should disappear, such as sessions and one-time tokens. Data that must be kept should not have a TTL.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when the bucket has no temporary documents.

options.label: On replace or upsert, keep the existing TTL when the document must still expire

risks.reason: By default, a replace or upsert without an explicit expiry resets the document expiry to 0, which means the document no longer expires on its own.

improvements.title: Preserve expiry on later writes
improvements.description: Consider the preserveExpiry option on replace, upsert, and mutateIn for documents whose lifetime depends on a TTL. It is available on Couchbase Server 7.0 and later.

options.guidance: This matters only for documents that use a TTL.

options.label: Store a schema version on the document and decide how old documents are updated

risks.reason: Old and new document shapes in the same collection cannot be told apart without a version field. Readers then fail or silently ignore fields.

improvements.title: Version the document shape
improvements.description: Consider adding a schema version field to documents and deciding whether old documents are upgraded when they are read or through a backfill.

questions.title: How do you balance SQL++ query consistency with performance?
questions.description: Scan consistency is chosen per query, so the wait is paid only where a query must see a specific write.

options.label: Choose scan consistency per query instead of one setting for the whole application

risks.reason: request_plus makes a query wait until the index has caught up with all writes, which is slower. not_bounded, the default, returns what the index has now and can miss a write the same session just made. One global setting is wrong for one of the two cases.

improvements.title: Set consistency on the query that needs it
improvements.description: Consider choosing scan consistency per query: not_bounded for reads that can be slightly behind, and request_plus or at_plus only for the queries that must see specific writes.

options.label: When a session must see its own write, pass the mutation token (at_plus) instead of using request_plus everywhere

risks.reason: request_plus waits for the index to catch up with every mutation in the cluster, not only the one made by this session.

improvements.title: Use at_plus for read-your-own-writes
improvements.description: When a session must see its own write, consider passing the mutation token from the write into the query (consistentWith / at_plus) rather than using request_plus everywhere.

questions.title: How do you maintain atomicity across multiple document modifications?
questions.description: One document is updated atomically by a single Key-Value write. Use a transaction only when one action must change several documents together.

options.label: Use Couchbase transactions when one action must commit several documents together

risks.reason: Separate writes can leave the first document updated and the second unchanged if the process stops in between.

improvements.title: Use a transaction for that action
improvements.description: When several documents must change together, consider Couchbase distributed ACID transactions through the SDK or SQL++. A home-made two-phase commit in application code is much harder to get right.

options.guidance: Leave this unchecked when each action updates one document.

options.label: Update one field with a Sub-Document call when you do not need to send the whole document

risks.reason: Rewriting a large document to change one field moves the whole document across the network and raises the chance of a CAS mismatch.

improvements.title: Use a Sub-Document update for one field
improvements.description: Consider mutateIn for a single-field change. Small documents can still be replaced in full.

options.label: Keep a transaction short, on a limited number of documents, and free of calls to other systems

risks.reason: A transaction that calls another service, or touches many documents, holds its resources until it commits or expires, and blocks other writers on those documents.

improvements.title: Shorten the transaction
improvements.description: Consider keeping transactions short, limited to the documents that must change together, and free of calls to external systems.

options.guidance: Only if the application uses Couchbase transactions.

options.label: Treat an ambiguous commit as unknown until you know whether it committed

risks.reason: A lost response after commit does not mean the transaction failed. Starting the business action again can apply it twice.

improvements.title: Handle an ambiguous commit
improvements.description: Consider treating a TransactionCommitAmbiguous result as unknown: check the data before retrying the business action. The transaction cleanup process completes or rolls back the transaction in the background.

options.guidance: Only if the application uses Couchbase transactions.

questions.guidance: If every business action changes one document, say so in the notes and leave the transaction items unchecked.

questions.title: How do you handle XDCR conflicts when both sites accept writes?
questions.description: Answer this only for active-active replication. A single cluster has no conflict mode to choose.

options.label: Choose the XDCR conflict mode when the bucket is created, and use the same mode on every bucket in the replication

risks.reason: The XDCR conflict-resolution mode is set when the bucket is created and cannot be changed later. Source and target buckets in a replication must use the same mode. Timestamp-based resolution depends on synchronized clocks; with clock drift it can keep the wrong version.

improvements.title: Decide the conflict mode before the bucket exists
improvements.description: Consider deciding between sequence-number and timestamp resolution before the bucket is created, and using the same choice on both sides of the replication. Timestamp resolution needs NTP on every node of both clusters.

options.guidance: You cannot change the mode later. Sequence number is the default. Timestamp mode is easier to reason about when NTP is on and clock drift is watched.
antiPatterns: Timestamp mode without NTP, or without watching clock drift
Replicating buckets that use different conflict modes

options.label: Filter XDCR so a remote cluster receives only the collections it needs

risks.reason: Replicating every collection sends data the other site may not be allowed to store, and uses bandwidth for nothing.

improvements.title: Filter the replication
improvements.description: Consider collection mapping or a filter expression on the replication, so a remote cluster receives only what it needs.

options.guidance: Only for an active-active or active-passive XDCR setup.

options.label: Turn on XDCR conflict logging when both clusters accept writes

risks.reason: Without a conflict log, you cannot see which document version was kept after a conflict.

improvements.title: Log XDCR conflicts
improvements.description: Consider enabling XDCR conflict logging when both clusters accept writes, and reviewing it when an application reports a lost update.

options.guidance: Only when both sides of the replication accept writes.

questions.guidance: Conflict resolution is chosen when the bucket is created and cannot be switched later.

questions.title: How do you automate complex data enrichment and reactive workflows?
questions.description: Use Eventing when a change in the cluster should run server-side logic. Do not build a private DCP client for a new workload.

options.label: Use an Eventing function for a reaction that should run inside the cluster

risks.reason: An application that polls for changes adds a steady read load. An Eventing function runs when a document changes.

improvements.title: Use Eventing for that reaction
improvements.description: Consider an Eventing function for reactions that belong inside the cluster, kept small and given a role limited to the collections it needs.

options.guidance: A worker outside the cluster, fed by the Kafka connector, is a valid alternative.

options.label: Use an Eventing timer for work that must run later, if you already use Eventing

risks.reason: A separate scheduler is extra machinery when an Eventing function already owns that workflow.

improvements.title: Use an Eventing timer
improvements.description: Consider an Eventing timer created from the function that owns the document. Adding Eventing only to get a timer is usually not worth it.

options.guidance: Only if you already run Eventing.

options.label: Give each Eventing function a role limited to the collections it uses

risks.reason: A function that runs with broad administrator privileges can change collections outside its purpose.

improvements.title: Limit the function's role
improvements.description: Consider a dedicated user for each Eventing function with access limited to the collections it reads and writes.

options.guidance: Only if you run Eventing.

options.label: Take a change feed from Eventing or a supported connector, not from a custom DCP client

risks.reason: The Database Change Protocol (DCP) is an internal protocol. A private DCP client has to handle flow control, failover, and rollback, which Eventing and the supported connectors already do.

improvements.title: Use a supported change feed
improvements.description: Consider Eventing or a supported connector such as the Kafka connector for change feeds, rather than a custom DCP consumer.

options.label: Use the same date, number, and enum formats in every SDK language that reads the documents

risks.reason: One service writing a string date and another writing an epoch number makes queries and comparisons disagree.

improvements.title: Publish the field formats
improvements.description: Consider agreeing the representation of dates, numbers, and enums across services, and checking it in review when a second language or SDK is added.

questions.guidance: Eventing is optional. The change-feed and data-format items apply to every application.
